package_info.why_malicious: This Excel document is specifically crafted to exploit CVE-2017-11882 by embedding a malicious OLE object that triggers a buffer overflow in EQNEDT32.EXE, resulting in arbitrary code execution. The exploit chain leads to the download and execution of further malware (Formbook/Redline), enabling data theft, persistence, and remote control of the victim's device.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the Excel application automatically loads and executes the embedded OLE object, which is designed to exploit a vulnerability in EQNEDT32.EXE, resulting in the execution of attacker-controlled code and initiating the malware infection chain.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Auto-loading OLE objects on document open, especially with randomized names and targeting known vulnerable components, is a well-documented malware delivery technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal Excel documents do not contain auto-loading OLE objects with randomized names that are crafted to exploit vulnerabilities in external components like EQNEDT32.EXE.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate OLE objects may be embedded for macros or interactive content, but not with autoLoad=true and not targeting the equation editor for code execution.
key_indicators: Randomized embedded OLE object file name

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During import-time, the shellcode executes within EQNEDT32.EXE, manipulates process memory, decrypts additional payloads, and prepares to download and execute further malware, resulting in full code execution under the victim's context.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Embedding shellcode in OLE objects to exploit memory corruption vulnerabilities is a hallmark of exploit-based malware. The code performs direct memory manipulation and API calls typical of exploitation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal OLE objects do not contain executable shellcode or attempt to manipulate process memory or call system APIs directly.
key_indicators: Obfuscated and decrypted code execution flow

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the decrypted shellcode uses Windows API calls to download an executable from a remote server, save it to disk, execute the downloaded file, and terminate the exploited process, enabling the next stage of the attack.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Downloading and executing remote binaries via shellcode is a classic malware delivery technique. The use of obfuscated shellcode and direct API calls to perform these actions is highly indicative of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate documents do not download and execute remote executables without explicit user consent or interaction.
key_indicators: URLDownloadToFileW API call to suspicious domain

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Extracts 'BBOKK' DLL from bitmap resource, decrypts and loads it in memory, then executes its entry point.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the dropper extracts an encrypted DLL from its bitmap resource, decrypts it in memory, loads the DLL without writing it to disk, and executes its entry point, continuing the infection chain without leaving obvious artifacts.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Extracting and executing code from resources, especially via in-memory loading, is a common malware evasion technique to avoid detection by file-based security solutions.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not typically decrypt and execute DLLs from bitmap resources in memory without clear user intent or transparency.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate packers or protectors may use resource-based loading for anti-tamper or licensing, but not for arbitrary code execution without user awareness.
key_indicators: Encrypted DLL stored in bitmap resource

execution_context.trigger: malware execution (runtime, after BBOKK DLL load)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: BBOKK DLL downloads Formbook payload from Discord CDN via InternetOpenUrlA(), decrypts it, and injects it into a randomly chosen system process (calc.exe, rasphone.exe, or cmd.exe) using process hollowing (CreateProcessW, VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, CreateRemoteThread).
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the in-memory DLL downloads an additional payload from Discord CDN, decrypts the payload, and injects it into a legitimate system process using process hollowing, enabling stealthy execution of the Formbook malware.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Downloading payloads from public CDNs and injecting them into system processes using process hollowing is a hallmark of advanced malware seeking to evade detection and gain persistence.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate DLLs do not download and inject code into unrelated system processes, especially not from public file-sharing services.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some security tools may use process injection for sandboxing or monitoring, but not for arbitrary payloads from untrusted sources.
key_indicators: Process hollowing of system binaries (calc.exe, rasphone.exe, cmd.exe)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Creates registry value under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run with value pointing to C:\Users\Public\Libraries\foyoqjbsL.url (Internet Shortcut) which launches C:\Users\Public\Libraries\Lsbjqoyof.exe (copied payload).
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the malware establishes persistence by creating a registry autorun entry under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, which points to an Internet Shortcut file that launches a disguised payload executable at system startup.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Creating autorun registry entries that point to disguised payloads via Internet Shortcut files is a classic malware persistence technique designed to evade casual detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate installers may create autorun entries, but not for files masquerading as Internet Shortcuts to local executables with obfuscated names.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate software may use autorun for updates or background services, but not with obfuscated file names and shortcut indirection to executables.
key_indicators: Registry Run key modification with obfuscated value
Internet Shortcut (.url) pointing to local executable

execution_context.file_location: Injected process (e.g., rasphone.exe, in-memory Formbook payload)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Sends HTTP GET requests to C2 server (e.g., hxxp[:]//www[.]waraporn[.]net/dy47/?Rt=...&nBZhXF=...) with Base64-encoded, encrypted stolen data.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the injected Formbook payload collects sensitive data from the victim's system, encrypts and Base64-encodes the data, and exfiltrates it to a remote C2 server via HTTP GET requests, enabling data theft and remote attacker control.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Exfiltrating data to remote C2 servers using encoded and encrypted payloads is a primary function of information-stealing malware like Formbook.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate processes do not send encrypted, encoded data to unknown external servers without user knowledge or consent.
key_indicators: HTTP GET requests with encoded data to C2 domains
Communication with known Formbook C2 infrastructure

attack_chain.action: Victim opens malicious Excel document, which auto-loads the embedded OLE object.
OLE object exploits CVE-2017-11882 in EQNEDT32.EXE, executing embedded shellcode.
Shellcode downloads and executes Formbook dropper from remote server.
Dropper extracts and loads BBOKK DLL from its resources, executing it in memory.
BBOKK DLL downloads Formbook payload from Discord CDN, decrypts it, and injects it into a legitimate system process using process hollowing.
BBOKK DLL establishes persistence by creating autorun registry entry pointing to disguised payload.
Injected Formbook payload collects and exfiltrates sensitive data to C2 servers.

behavioral_signatures: Excel documents containing auto-loading OLE objects with autoLoad=true targeting EQNEDT32.EXE
Shellcode execution during OLE object parsing in Office processes
Abnormal API calls such as URLDownloadToFileW or WinExec from Office or EQNEDT32.EXE processes
In-memory DLL extraction and execution from bitmap or other resources
Process hollowing of system binaries (calc.exe, rasphone.exe, cmd.exe) by non-standard parent processes
Registry Run key modifications with values pointing to Internet Shortcut files (.url) that launch local executables with obfuscated names
HTTP GET requests with Base64-encoded, encrypted data to known Formbook C2 domains
file_indicators: BBOKK DLL present only in memory (not on disk)
network_indicators: Additional C2 domains as listed in the report's IOC section
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Office documents containing auto-loading OLE objects, especially those referencing EQNEDT32.EXE. Detect shellcode execution or abnormal API calls (e.g., URLDownloadToFileW, WinExec) from Office or EQNEDT32.EXE processes. Watch for process hollowing activity targeting system binaries, in-memory DLL loading from resources, and suspicious registry Run key modifications pointing to Internet Shortcut files with obfuscated names. Network monitoring should flag downloads from known malware distribution domains and C2 communications with encoded payloads. Correlate these behaviors for high-confidence detection of this attack chain.
